sections.title: How does the Board on board fence calculator work?
sections.html:
The Board on board fence calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports number of posts in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the fence length, the post space, the fence height and number of rails.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Board on board fence calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Number of posts=rounded up, ((fence length + post space) ÷ post space)
Number of sections=rounded up, (fence length ÷ post space)
Rails per section=number of rails ÷ rounded up, (fence length ÷ post space)
Number of pickets=rounded up, ((-fence length + picket overlapping) ÷ (picket overlapping − picket width))
Post length=(3 ÷ 2) × fence height

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Fence length = 30 m, Post space = 30 m, Rails per section = 2 and Picket width = 30 cm. The calculator returns Number of posts = 2, Number of sections = 1 and Number of rails = 2.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Number of posts = 2, Number of sections = 1 and Number of rails = 2 should be roughly the size you expected from Fence length = 30 m and Post space = 30 m.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Board on board fence calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Checking a supplier's figure against your own measurements
  • Ordering material and not wanting a second trip
  • Quoting a job where areas and quantities drive the price
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the fence length, the post space and the fence height — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Board on board fence calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns number of posts, derived from the fence length, the post space and the fence height. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Board on board fence calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the fence length, the post space, the fence height and number of rails, which is 6 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter fence length in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Fence length opens in meters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Number of posts = 2. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Board on board fence calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
